headline: Mackerel Push Bass Shallow: 49-Inch Fish Off Plymouth, Flounder Working Deer Island Flat
subhead: With bait schools running thick off the South Shore, I sent my week south instead of north — here's why, and where the harbor still delivered.
body_markdown:
I had a choice to make Monday morning — run the harbor islands like I usually do this time of year, or point south toward Plymouth and Duxbury where word was mackerel schools have been rolling thick along the beach. I went south first. When mackerel show in numbers like they have the last ten days, big bass follow them right up onto the bars, and a fish pushing 49 inches doesn't come from nowhere. That's the kind of intel that changes a week's plan.

The South Shore didn't disappoint, but it wasn't a layup either. Duxbury Bay and the outer edge of Plymouth Beach have had pods of mackerel stacking up on the last two hours of the incoming, and where the bait bunches against the bar, the bass have been sitting underneath waiting. Best presentation has been a bare mackerel jig dropped through the school to snag a live one, then free-lined back with just enough weight to keep it down near bottom in 15 to 20 feet. No wire, no heavy leader — these fish are eating naturally and they know the difference. The 40-inch-plus class has come almost entirely on live mackerel fished this way, right at first light before the boat traffic stirs things up. By mid-morning the bite goes quiet and stays that way until the tide turns again in the evening. That's the pattern — two windows a day, tide-driven, and if you're not there for the window you're just burning gas.

Back in the harbor, Deer Island continues to do what it always does for me in mid-July — flounder on the flat and bass off the drop. The channel edge on the north side of Deer Island Light drops from eight feet down to better than 30 in a short run, and on the outgoing tide that edge holds bait that gets pushed off the flat. I've been anchoring up-current of the drop and drifting sandworms and clam bellies on a simple two-hook flounder rig for a mixed bag — nothing huge, but a fifteen-fish morning isn't unusual right now if you hit dead low through the first hour of the outgoing. Once the current really starts moving, I switch over and work bucktails — half-ounce white with a chunk of pork rind — along the same drop for bass. They're not stacked up thick, but there's a resident population working that ledge all summer and a couple of keepers most trips isn't a bad return for an hour's work.

Spectacle Island has been slower than I'd like it. The water on the flats around there has warmed enough that the bigger bass have mostly moved off into deeper water during the day, and what's left is smaller fish picking at green crabs and worms in close to the rocks. I'm not writing it off completely — an evening tide change with some current still moving can produce, but I wouldn't make it my first stop right now.

Nahant has been more consistent, especially the rocks on the east side toward the Causeway. Bass have been holding tight to structure there on the last of the incoming, ambushing whatever gets pushed against the ledges. Topwater plugs at dusk have worked well — a Danny-style swimmer worked slow across the surface has drawn some good strikes in that last hour of light. Nothing over 34 inches that I've seen personally, but a lot of mid-20s to low-30s fish, and that's a fun bite on light spinning gear.

Up on Cape Ann, the story's been about bluefish more than bass this week. Gloucester Harbor and the rocks around Rockport have had blues chopping bait on the surface during the middle of the day — not the giant class, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but plenty of them, and they'll hit anything shiny moving fast. Small metal jigs, half-ounce Kastmasters, cast into the working birds has been the easiest way to get bit. Bass fishing along the Cape Ann ledges has been quieter — a few fish coming off the deeper structure off Straitsmouth on the dropping tide, but it's been a fish here, a fish there, not a pattern I'd build a whole trip around yet.

Water's comfortable right now across the whole zone — warm in the shallow harbor flats, a touch cooler out along the open ledges off Cape Ann, which is typical for mid-July. Tides have been moving well without any big extremes, which keeps these current-edge bites predictable if you're willing to work around the clock rather than fish whenever's convenient.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd keep my attention on the South Shore as long as those mackerel schools hold. If the bait pushes offshore or breaks up, the big bass will follow it, and Plymouth and Duxbury could go quiet fast — that's happened before in past summers when a bait pod moves overnight. In the harbor, Deer Island should keep producing flounder on the outgoing as long as the current keeps sweeping that flat clean, and I expect Nahant's dusk topwater bite to hold steady through the week if the wind stays manageable. If you've only got one trip in you, I'd fish the early incoming at Plymouth Beach with a mackerel jig rigged and ready — but I'd have Deer Island as my backup if the bait doesn't show.
